newsitem.title: ROMANIA: World Bank loan seen boosting Romania's image.
newsitem.headline: World Bank loan seen boosting Romania's image.

text.p: Analysts on Thursday welcomed this week's World Bank pledge to extend $625 million in credits to Romania, saying it would boost the world banking community's confidence in the country, help growth and promote investment.
"The World Bank gesture will reverberate within the international financial and banking milieu, boosting Romania's image and position," independent economist Doru Nicolaescu said.

World Bank President James Wolfensohn said the Bank had agreed to give Romania almost twice the money it was expecting. He said the loans reflected the Bank's confidence in the government's reform programme.

Romania's new centrist leadership, which ousted leftists in last November's elections, launched a tough reform package in February. Earlier proposals for World Bank loans had provided for some $300 million plus $80 million in resumed funds under an earlier Financial and Enterprise Structural Adjustment Loan.
All credits are subject to Bank board approval next month.

"Any bank checks out a potential debtor's payment capacity before giving it a loan. If the World Bank agreed to give credits to Romania it means it implictly trusts its potential for economic growth," Nicolaescu said.
Romania's image has improved since the elections as the centrist coalition promised to deliver on plans to step up privatisation and encourage foreign investors.
The government submitted an austerity budget and also rushed laws on bank privatisation and foreign owership of land through parliament.

"The government's positive actions have sent signs of reassurance to foreign investors," another local economist said. "Underpinning loans from both the World Bank and the IMF is further reassurance."
Last month, the International Monetary Fund approved credits totalling $430 million for Romania.

"The IMF loan was a confirmation that the Fund was backing up Romania," a Western analyst said. "The picture was rounded off by World Bank funds. I notice growing interest (in Romania) from both direct and portfolio investors around me."
Both the World Bank and the IMF suspended credits in 1996, complaining the leftist cabinet had overshot spending targets.
"Another advantage of the World Bank loan is that it is aimed at sectors of public interest. Putting the money to work in these areas will help economic growth," Nicolaescu said.

The World Bank credit includes $350 million for an Agricultural Structural Adjustment Loan, $50 million for social programmes, $150 million to upgrade roads, $50 million for higher education and $25 million to improve water supplies.
